name: High-Wrist Guillotine
keyCorrections: If the choke doesn't feel clean, your wrist is not deep enough — slide the wrist blade deeper on their neck.
If they posture out, your elbow is not tight enough — clamp the elbow to your body.
If you can't finish, your angle is too square — step further to their side.
description: A guillotine variation using a deep wrist blade position and precise elbow control for a cleaner, tighter finish against opponents who defend the standard guillotine.
shortInstruction: Deep wrist blade on the neck, elbow tight to the ribs, head to the side — the high-wrist guillotine cuts deeper than the standard grip.
summary: The high-wrist guillotine (also called the Marcelotine or Japanese guillotine) uses the blade of your wrist against the carotid artery rather than the standard biceps-squeeze grip. The key is that your wrist is positioned deeper on their neck — the blade of your forearm (thumb side) presses directly into their carotid. This variation is more effective in no-gi because it does not require a gi collar grip and creates a tighter blood choke with less effort.
whyItWorks: The wrist blade creates more direct pressure on the carotid artery than the standard forearm squeeze.
The high-wrist position allows you to finish from angles where the standard guillotine would not work.
It is more effective in no-gi because it does not depend on fabric grips.
Danaher/Marcelo Garcia principle: the high wrist is the no-gi evolution of the guillotine — it uses bone pressure, not fabric friction.
commonMistakes: Using the flat of the wrist instead of the blade (thumb side) — the blade creates the choke, the flat creates a crank.
Not keeping the elbow tight to your body — a flared elbow gives them space to posture.
Pulling horizontally instead of cutting the angle — the high wrist works best with a sharp angle cut.
Squeezing too early before the wrist is deep — deep wrist first, then angle, then squeeze.
coachingCues: Wrist blade, not flat — the thumb side creates the choke.
Elbow tight, angle sharp, wrist deep.
If you can feel your wrist on their spine, you're deep enough.
The high wrist is a scalpel — the standard guillotine is a hammer.
safetySummary: The high wrist can create more focused pressure on the neck — apply gradually and respect the tap.
Do not crank the neck to force the choke — it is a blood choke, not a neck crank.
If the opponent taps to neck pressure rather than choke sensation, release immediately.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Front headlock or guard: deep wrist grip (thumb side blade) → elbow tight → cut angle → squeeze with chest.

decisionTree.action: The high-wrist guillotine works best from the front headlock position when they are turtled or belly down.

decisionTree.condition: they defend by hiding their neck

moneyDetails: Grip their neck with your palm facing up — the blade of your forearm (thumb side) should be against their carotid.
Your elbow must be touching your own ribs — a tight elbow is what prevents them from posturing.
Cut the angle by stepping to the side of their head — the sharper the angle, the tighter the choke.
Finish by bringing your elbow toward your hip while keeping the wrist blade deep — this rotates the blade into their neck.
nextStep: After the high-wrist guillotine, learn the standard guillotine system and Marcelotine details.
fixItFast: Choke not clean? Rotate your wrist so the blade (thumb side) presses into their neck.
They keep posturing? Step further to their side and tighten your elbow to your ribs.
Wrist keeps slipping? Re-grip deeper — the wrist should reach the back of their neck, not just the side.
